title: How AI is changing Software Engineering: A Conversation with Gergely Orosz, @The Pragmatic Engineer
talk_summary: A fireside chat with Gergely Orosz about how AI is changing software engineering, focused mostly on organizational culture: 'token maxing' at big tech, productivity measurement, changing engineer roles, and why large companies build internal AI infra. It contains almost no concrete agent-orchestration techniques, but a few transferable lessons about measurement incentives, context limits, and internal tooling.

takeaways.technique: Avoid token-spend as a productivity metric
takeaways.what_they_do: Companies rank engineers by token spend, so people burn tokens on useless agent runs to avoid looking like low performers; the metric drives waste, not output.
takeaways.evidence_quote: people are just running autonomous agents to build junk honestly for the sake of having that number go up
takeaways.numbers: Salesforce minimum spend ~$175/month per person; Meta leaderboard removed after press

takeaways.technique: Custom retrieval over huge repos beats off-the-shelf context
takeaways.what_they_do: Big companies build custom background agents and MCP gateways integrated with their monorepo because their code never fits a context window; bespoke tooling gives better results than vendor tools.
takeaways.evidence_quote: these companies have such so much code that never fit in a context window, by building custom solutions ... they will have better results than off-the-shelf vendors

takeaways.technique: Internal MCP gateway as shared infra
takeaways.what_they_do: Companies route all agent tool access through one MCP gateway wired into service discovery and internal tooling, rather than each agent integrating tools ad hoc.
takeaways.evidence_quote: If you're at a large company and you're not already building an MCP gateway, what are you even doing?

takeaways.what_they_do: Uber's internal code review system categorizes changes by risk, so review effort and automation are allocated by risk rather than uniformly.
takeaways.evidence_quote: their internal code review system is like like categorizing based on risk

takeaways.what_they_do: Instead of only making engineers faster, give non-coding collaborators agent access so they can produce changes without waiting on an engineer.
Practitioners converge on running only one or two agents at a time rather than many; orchestration feels like a mech suit, not people management.
